strengths: The proposed task is practically motivated, and ITCPR provides a potentially useful resource: 2,202 composed queries and a 20,510-image gallery drawn from three person-retrieval datasets. Manual relative captions and an additional pass to recover missing positives are valuable contributions.

The results demonstrate benefits beyond encoder fine-tuning alone. With ViT-L/14, Word4Per achieves 45.55% Rank-1 and 55.26% mAP, compared with 32.02% and 41.83% for image–text averaging using the same fine-tuned encoders.

The two-stage pipeline is understandable and computationally practical. Training settings, losses, and inference templates are described, and the supplementary material adds useful experiments on architecture, training data, fusion, and runtime. The paper also explicitly acknowledges its limited treatment of stable identity features.
weaknesses: The headline comparison with Pic2Word is insufficiently controlled. Table 1 explicitly states that its mapper was trained with original CLIP parameters, including when evaluated with fine-tuned encoders. This representation mismatch confounds the reported advantage. Table 2 provides a useful partial control on ViT-B/16, but the large ViT-L/14 superiority claim still requires retraining Pic2Word with matched encoders and person data. The other cited textual-inversion approach [2] is also not evaluated.

The methodological advance is modest and insufficiently distinguished from prior work: the framework combines existing person-retrieval fine-tuning, Pic2Word-style pseudo-token composition, and established matching losses. This makes the task and benchmark the strongest potential contribution, but their validation is not yet convincing enough to carry the paper.

The evaluation does not adequately establish identity-sensitive retrieval. Section 4.1 deliberately favors pairs retaining some clothing similarity, while results are aggregated across all three source datasets. Comparisons with strong clothes-changing person-retrieval methods, per-source results, and tests involving similar-looking impostors or extensive clothing changes would help establish whether the method preserves identity beyond matching appearance attributes. Annotation agreement and the coverage of the missing-positive search are also undocumented.

The model-selection protocol is unclear. ITCPR is described as exclusively for testing, yet supplementary Sections C.3–C.5 select optimal architectures and fusion configurations from its results without identifying an independent validation procedure. This raises concerns about optimistic optimized results. Missing seed variability also limits confidence in smaller ablation and fusion improvements.

The stated surveillance and public-security applications, together with planned redistribution of person imagery, warrant discussion of privacy, source permissions, and potential misuse. The manuscript does not document these considerations; this is a reporting concern, not evidence of an established ethical violation.
